lines: Remember the last time your face went hot? You said the wrong thing, stumbled over a word, or tried something in front of people, and it did not go well.
Most of us will do almost anything to avoid that feeling. We stay quiet. We skip the audition, the question, the message. We stay safely in the middle.
The actor Austin Butler put it like this: embarrassment is an underexplored emotion. Go out there and make a fool of yourself, because everything you want is on the other side of it.
There is a deep truth in that, and research can help us see exactly what it is.
This film is about shame and embarrassment. What they really are, and why learning to move through them may be one of the most transformative things you can do.

First, what are these feelings for? Humans are built to belong. In a landmark review, Roy Baumeister and Mark Leary concluded that the need to belong is a powerful, fundamental, and extremely pervasive motivation.
Embarrassment seems to be part of that system. Researchers describe it as a kind of nonverbal apology. A signal that says: I know I broke a norm, and I care about this relationship.
So when your face goes hot, an alarm is going off. And the alarm is not really about the mistake. It is about your place in the group.
That may be why it feels so enormous. As if being seen as foolish could cost you your belonging.
So the key question is: is the alarm accurate?
It helps to separate three things that often get tangled together. Embarrassment, guilt, and shame.
Embarrassment is about a moment. Something happened in front of others, and it passes. Researchers treat it as a distinct emotion.
Guilt says: I did something wrong. It points at the behavior, and tends to push us toward making amends.
Shame says: I am something wrong. It points at the whole self, and tends to push us toward hiding.
That difference matters. In a meta-analysis, shame was more strongly linked to anxiety symptoms than guilt was. And in one set of studies, guilt motivated amends, while shame motivated evasion.
So the work is not to feel nothing. It is to keep the embarrassment and the guilt, and loosen shame's verdict that you are the problem.
Now, is the alarm accurate? Try an experiment. Imagine walking into a room wearing an embarrassing T-shirt.
In a classic set of studies, people who wore one overestimated how many others would be able to recall what was on it. This is called the spotlight effect.
We anchor on our own vivid experience of our mistakes, and adjust too little for the fact that everyone else is busy managing their own.
The same bias makes us think our ups and downs are noticed far more than they are. The researchers linked it to social anxiety, and to the regrets of things we never tried.
There is even a practical trick. In experiments, imagining an upcoming event from a third person view, or far in the future, reduced the spotlight effect and the embarrassment.
Most people are not watching you as closely as it feels. They are busy standing in their own spotlight.
And when people do notice, what do they think? Often, better of you than you expect.
In experiments, people who showed embarrassment after a mistake were rated as more prosocial and more trustworthy, and others wanted to affiliate with them and share resources.

In six preregistered studies with over three thousand people, those who laughed at a harmless mistake were seen as warmer, more competent, and more authentic than those who showed embarrassment. When a mistake hurts someone, though, taking it seriously matters.
We also underestimate how willing people are to help. In a series of studies, people underestimated by as much as fifty percent how likely others were to agree to a direct request for help.
And helpers feel better about helping than the person asking expects.
So asking, trying, and being seen mid attempt costs less than the alarm predicts.
Meanwhile, avoiding embarrassment has a price. And we rarely count it.
Shame drives hiding. In a workplace study, people who felt shame after hiding knowledge tended to withdraw, while guilt led them to make up for it by helping others.

In learning environments, shame and humiliation inhibit speaking up and asking questions. Psychologically safe environments, where people are not punished for mistakes, are linked to more speaking up and more learning from failure.
And over a lifetime, people tend to regret what they did not do more than what they did. Replications mostly support this pattern, though with weaker effects, and with some differences.
Every unasked question, unsent message, and unsung song is a small vote for staying exactly where you are.
So what is on the other side? Start with what facing the feared thing does.

Therapists treat social anxiety with exposure, gradually approaching the situations a person fears. In a meta-analysis of thirty trials of exposure delivered in virtual reality, across anxiety disorders including social anxiety, effects were large compared with waiting, and similar to real world exposure.
A newer trial gave people with social anxiety web based therapy, and added a part aimed at shame itself. That version reduced both shame and social anxiety more than the standard version.

And in a review of treatments for internalized shame, most showed small to moderate reductions, often through education, experiential exercises, and social support. The studies are early, but the direction is hopeful.
Now think about what else lives on that side. The friendship you start by saying hello. The skill you learn by being bad at it. The love you find by saying it. The help you get by asking.
Almost everything worth having begins with a moment of looking foolish.
But you cannot wish shame away. The way through is not to fight it. It is to stay with it, kindly.
In one experiment, people recalled a shame memory and then did a short exercise. The self compassion exercise reduced shame more than the control.
And in a study of nearly four hundred students, self compassion softened the link between external shame, the fear of being judged by others, and depression and anxiety.
Try this the next time your face goes hot. First, name it. This is embarrassment.
Second, remind yourself that it is human. Everyone feels this. Plenty of people have stood exactly where you are standing.
Third, speak to yourself like a friend. That was awkward, and I am still okay.
And tell one safe person. Treatments for shame often include social support and emotional expression. If your shame runs deep, or comes from something painful, a therapist can help you go slowly.
So what is the deep truth in Austin Butler's words?
Shame guards the door of everything new. It says: if you try this and fail where people can see, you will lose your place.
But belonging was never built on being flawless. It is built on connection. The need to belong is a need for frequent, caring interactions, not for perfect performances.
When you can survive being seen as foolish, you stop spending your life protecting an image. And you become free to try, to ask, to love, and to learn.
Embarrassment is not a sign that something is wrong. Often it is simply the feeling of growing, in public.
The cost of never being seen as a beginner is never becoming anything else.
Here is a week of small, safe fool making.
One. List five mildly embarrassing things you avoid. Rate each from one to ten.
Two. Pick one at a three or four. Ask the question you think is silly. Sing a little off key. Admit you do not know.
Three. Before you do it, say: embarrassment is a sign I am growing. Afterwards, notice what actually happened.
Four. Check the evidence. How many people noticed? How did they respond?
Five. Say one kind sentence to yourself, and tell one friend. Next week, try a five.
And right now, take one slow breath. Think of one thing you have been avoiding. You do not have to do it today. Just picture the other side of it.
You are allowed to be a beginner.
You are allowed to be seen trying.
Go out there, and be a little foolish. Everything you want is on the other side.
Thank you for watching.
The research behind this film is listed on screen.
